article_title: Sheriff Baldwin says Franklin County jails contacting ICE not new
article_content:
How Franklin County jails cooperate with immigration enforcement
- Franklin County jails proactively notify federal immigration officials about all detainees born outside the U.S., even citizens.
- The Sheriff's Office policy states it does not honor civil ICE holds, which are non-binding requests.
- However, local attorneys and court records suggest the jail holds people for ICE past their release date.
- Immigrant advocates decry the jail policy as going beyond what’s required. Sheriff Dallas Baldwin defended the policy, saying it’s not new.
The Franklin County jails are cooperating with federal immigration officials and at times, hold people past when they've paid bond or their criminal case is dismissed, according to court records and local immigration attorneys.
The Franklin County Sheriff's jail staff for years have asked during booking where a detainee was born and proactively called Immigration and Customs Enforcement about all immigrants – anyone simply born outside the U.S., which could include citizens and other immigrants with legal status.
If ICE requests to be notified of an immigrant's pending release from the jail, Franklin County Sheriff Dallas Baldwin's office calls ICE.
While this has been policy in Franklin County for years, ICE under President Donald Trump has been more aggressive about hitting arrest quotas. ICE picked up more than 50 people from the Franklin County jails in the first half of 2025, according to the latest available data. In all of 2024, ICE picked up 11 people at the Franklin County jails.
By policy Columbus police do not work with ICE, and the courts in Franklin County have moved to restrict ICE arrests on site.
Baldwin, a Democrat who took office in 2017, told The Dispatch in an emailed response that everyone is entitled to their opinion about jail policy.
“However, this policy is not new — it reflects a longstanding practice our office has maintained in coordination with federal authorities for many years," Baldwin said. "It’s also important to note that the information referenced is already a matter of public record.”
The policy on ICE notifications, which was provided to The Dispatch, predates Baldwin, according to Baldwin's spokesperson, Maria Durant.
Testifying at a Columbus City Council hearing in February, former council member and YWCA Columbus President Elizabeth Brown urged council to dig into how Columbus police and Franklin County law enforcement create a pipeline to ICE detaining vulnerable people arrested for minor charges. The Dispatch looked into it.
Franklin County jails proactively notify ICE about all immigrants
According to the Sheriff Office's policy on ICE notifications, jail staff notifies ICE for a list of reasons. This includes when the detainee speaks little English, does not have a government-issued identification, requires consular notification or simply was born outside of the U.S.
David Dawson, a Columbus immigration attorney at Simakovsky Law, said the Sheriff's Office is under no obligation by federal or state law to proactively notify ICE directly like the office is doing.
"They're basically trying to feed people to ICE," said Lynn Tramonte, director of the Ohio Immigration Alliance. "They're giving ICE a bunch of junk, a bunch of people who are probably not even undocumented ... and there's no requirement for them to do that. They’re definitely targeting people based on national origin and ethnicity."
Tramonte said local law enforcement can't leave it up to ICE to do the right thing and only arrest people they're legally allowed to arrest.
"ICE is arresting every person they can," she said. "They don’t care if this person is currently deportable or not."
Tramonte said ICE is putting people into detention centers in poor conditions, whether or not they have a work permit or open asylum case, so people will get desperate and agree to self-deport.
Franklin jails holding people past release dates, records show and attorneys say
ICE detainers, sometimes called ICE holds or immigration holds, ask local law enforcement to notify ICE before a person is released and/or hold a person past when they're supposed to be released up to 48 hours so ICE can pick them up. These are nonbinding requests filed with local law enforcement, said Dawson.
Not every jail across the country complies with civil ICE holds. The Hennepin County Sheriff Dawana Witt's Office in Minneapolis does not honor civil immigration detainers in the jail there and has defended the policy as legal against a lawsuit brought by the U.S. Department of Justice.
On paper, the Franklin County jails also do not honor ICE detainers. Durant said in an email the Sheriff's Office wanted to note this line of the policy:
“Regardless of ICE detainers, once an inmate has been fully processed for release, they are released from the Sheriff’s custody; under no circumstances are they held or maintained in custody without current criminal charges.”
Durant clarified that the Franklin County Sheriff's Office honors criminal detainers, but not civil detainers requested by ICE.
But people are regularly held in the Franklin County jails on ICE detainers and handed over to ICE, according to court records and local attorneys.
The vast majority of ICE detainers are civil in nature, said Dawson, and criminal detainers usually involve an agency other than ICE.
Robert Wisniewski, a Columbus immigration attorney at The Nemecek Firm, told The Dispatch anecdotally that the sheriff's office violated its policy and honored a civil ICE hold on his client in April 2025.
"I’ve personally had a client where their immigration case was 100% civil and the Franklin County jail kept her after her criminal case was dismissed so that ICE could pick her up," Wisniewski told The Dispatch. "It was well after her criminal case was dismissed and well after 48 hours later."
That client was seeking asylum in the U.S. after she was attacked in her home country, Wisniewski said. It was difficult for the woman to gather evidence while being held in detention for ICE and she lost her case. She could have appealed, but after eight months in the Butler County Jail, where Wisniewski said conditions were very hard on her, the woman gave up and allowed herself to be deported.
She left behind a husband and child in the U.S.
"She’s in danger in her country. She was attacked by people with knives and machetes and medical records say she had to have 40 stitches in her back," Wisniewski said of the attack that brought his client to the U.S. "Had she been released from the Franklin County jail, we probably would’ve appealed, we probably would’ve fought and who knows what would’ve happened."
Government and politics reporter Jordan Laird can be reached at jlaird@dispatch.com. Follow her on X, Instagram and Bluesky at @LairdWrites.
